1324.title: The replication crisis
1324.hook: in 2015 only about 36 percent of a hundred psychology studies replicated clearly (Open Science Collaboration)
1324.howItsDone: Researchers check a finding by running the same study again, often with new teams and larger groups; a result that holds up across repeats is trusted more than a single striking study.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the section on compassion with a farmer who tugged his grain. Your line was it grows: tended, slowly, without force.

A hundred psychology studies, already published in respected journals, were run a second time. Same questions, same methods, as close as the new teams could get, often with help from the original authors. Nearly all the originals had reported a clear result. The repeats? About 36 percent did. That came from a large group of researchers calling themselves the Open Science Collaboration. This path has spent weeks sharing findings from labs, so it owes you this part too. A new section starts today: the honest part.
screen: `A HUNDRED STUDIES, RUN AGAIN.` → `ABOUT 36 PERCENT HELD CLEARLY.` → `THE HONEST PART BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, what was done. The point wasn't to catch anyone out. It was a plain question: if you do the same study again, do you get the same answer? The teams repeated each study once, carefully, and published everything, including the misses. Second, what came back. Only about a third of the repeats showed a clear result, and where an effect did show up again, it was often smaller than first reported. Third, what that does and doesn't mean. A failed repeat doesn't prove the original was wrong, and it certainly doesn't prove anyone cheated. A single repeat can miss too. What it means is humbler: one study is a first word, not a last word. A finding earns trust by surviving being done again, by other people, in other places. Fourth, an old line that already knew this. The book of Proverbs, in the King James text, says: "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him." The first account tends to sound right. Then the neighbor arrives and checks. Replication is the neighbor. And it applies here: many findings this path has shared were single studies, and a few came with a note that later work was mixed. That's no reason to throw them out. It's a reason to hold them like any first account: with interest, and a question ready.
screen: `ASK THE SAME QUESTION TWICE.` · `ABOUT A THIRD HELD UP CLEARLY.` · `ONE STUDY IS A FIRST WORD.` · `THE NEIGHBOR COMES TO CHECK.` · then, large: `WAS IT REPEATED?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one finding you've taken on board, from this path, a headline or a friend: phones make us dumber, gratitude makes us happier, whatever comes. Hold it for a few breaths and ask quietly: was it repeated? If you don't know, let the not-knowing sit beside the finding without pushing either one away.
The replication crisis. When psychology repeated its own studies, many results came back weaker or didn't come back at all. Today's word.
Your line: was it repeated? It's a kind question, not a cynical one. I'll be here tomorrow.

1325.title: What held up
1325.hook: sleep, exercise, social ties and practice effects have strong support
1325.howItsDone: Health researchers trust findings that many independent studies agree on, gathered in reviews that pool them; sleep, physical activity and social connection are among the findings with this kind of support.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the replication crisis: a hundred studies run again, and only about a third holding clearly. Your line was was it repeated.

So, after yesterday, is anything left standing? The wrong conclusion is easy to reach: if famous findings shrank or vanished, maybe none of it means anything. Go to bed whenever. Skip the walk. Cancel the dinner. That isn't what the record shows. Some findings have been tested over and over, by different teams, in different countries, with different methods, and pooled together in large reviews. They don't make headlines anymore, because they're old news. Today is the old news: the boring findings that held up.
screen: `IS ANYTHING LEFT STANDING?` → `TESTED OVER AND OVER.` → `THE BORING FINDINGS.`

segments.voice: First, sleep. A review that pooled studies of lost sleep found a clear pattern: short on sleep, people think, remember and manage their moods worse. A Psalm in the King James text says it gently: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Sleep there is a gift, not a reward for finishing everything. Second, moving your body. Exercise has been tested against low mood in many trials, and reviews find it helps, though how much varies from study to study. Third, other people. A large review led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad pooled studies on social relationships and found that people with stronger ties tended to live longer. Ecclesiastes saw the shape of it: "woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." Fourth, practice itself, modestly. A large review of meditation programs, led by Madhav Goyal, found moderate evidence that they eased anxiety, depression and pain a little. Not a cure, and not shown to beat other active treatments, like exercise. But it held up. What the four share: none is new, none is a trick, and each has been checked by the neighbor many times and is still standing. Not one bright study, but many ordinary ones agreeing.

segments.voice: Let the four come up one at a time: sleep, movement, people, practice. Notice, without judging, which one your life is shortest on right now. Then picture the smallest real version of it, lights out a little earlier, a walk around the block, a message to one friend, and let that picture settle with the breath.
What held up. Sleep, movement, social ties and practice: findings tested over and over that are still standing. Today's word.
Your line: what held up. The boring findings are the sturdy ones, and they do their work quietly. Until tomorrow.

1326.title: Too many good results
1326.hook: meditation trials report more positive results than expected by chance (Coronado-Montoya et al., 2016)
1326.howItsDone: Researchers check for missing studies by comparing published trials with public trial registries and with how many positive results the studies' size would predict; researchers can also announce trials in public registries before running them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was what held up: sleep, movement, other people, and practice, modestly. Your line was what held up.

There's a drawer in this story. A researcher runs a careful trial of a meditation program: months of work. The result comes back flat, no clear difference between the people who meditated and the people who didn't. It's honest, it's dull, and it's hard to get anyone excited about printing it. So the paper goes into a drawer, and the researcher moves on. Nobody lied. Nobody cheated. Now multiply that drawer across a whole field. What reaches the public is the pile of studies that worked, and the pile looks wonderful. Today, a team counted it.
screen: `A CAREFUL TRIAL, A FLAT RESULT.` → `INTO THE DRAWER.` → `THE PILE THAT REACHES US.`

segments.voice: First, the question. A team led by Stephanie Coronado-Montoya looked at published trials of mindfulness-based therapies and asked something clever. Not, does it work? But: given how big these studies were, how many should come out positive, even if mindfulness really helps? Small studies miss real effects fairly often, so a healthy record should include some misses. Second, the answer. The published trials reported positive results far more often than their size would predict. Too many good results: the fingerprint of missing studies. Third, where the missing ones went. The team also checked trial registries, public lists where researchers announce a study before running it. A good share of registered trials had not been published long after they finished. The drawer is real. Fourth, what this does and doesn't mean. It doesn't mean meditation does nothing; yesterday's review still found modest benefits. It means the published picture is probably rosier than the full one, and the honest size of the effect is likely smaller than the brightest papers suggest. Paul, writing to the church at Thessalonica, put the posture plainly, in the King James text: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Test first, then hold on. Not a cynic, who throws everything out, and not a fan, who keeps everything. Someone in the middle, with a question ready.
screen: `HOW MANY SHOULD COME OUT POSITIVE?` · `FAR MORE THAN EXPECTED.` · `THE DRAWER IS REAL.` · `ROSIER THAN THE FULL PICTURE.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing this path, or any app, book or teacher, has told you practice will do for you: calmer, kinder, sharper. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold a bird, and ask two things: what would it look like if this weren't true for me, and what have I actually noticed? Let both answers be allowed, and keep sitting either way.
Too many good results. When nearly every published trial is positive, some of the flat ones are probably in a drawer. Today's word.
Your line: a little sceptical. A good question is its own kind of respect. That's today, done.

1327.title: Mindfulness without ethics
1327.hook: critics warn that mindfulness sold for productivity can lose its Buddhist ethical roots (Purser, 2019)
1327.howItsDone: In Buddhist teaching, mindfulness is practiced as one part of the eightfold path alongside right speech, action and livelihood; some secular teachers also pair mindfulness practice with an ethical intention for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was too many good results, and the drawer where flat studies go. Your line was a little sceptical.

A calendar invite lands in a work inbox: Mindfulness for peak performance. Twelve noon, conference room B, lunch provided. Breathe, focus, reduce stress, get more done. Nothing wrong with any of that. But one critic asks a sharper question. What if the stress is coming from something that ought to change? A schedule nobody can meet. A boss who shouts. Then a practice that only teaches you to stay calm might be helping the problem stay put. Today, that worry, and where mindfulness came from before it reached the conference room.
screen: `MINDFULNESS FOR PEAK PERFORMANCE.` → `WHAT IF THE STRESS SHOULD CHANGE?` → `WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: First, the critique. Ronald Purser, a business professor and Buddhist teacher, wrote a book with a pointed title: McMindfulness. He argues that mindfulness sold for productivity can be cut off from its roots, so it helps people adjust calmly to whatever is wearing them down, without asking whether that thing is right. Calm, he says, isn't the same as good. Second, the roots. In the Buddha's first teaching, as the tradition records it, right mindfulness is one part of an eightfold path, beside right speech, right action and right livelihood: how you talk, how you act, how you earn a living. Mindfulness there is one strand braided with the others, not a tool that floats free. Third, a line that holds the strands together. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind." Purifying the mind comes last, after not harming and doing good. Fourth, the other side, fairly. Defenders of secular programs say leaving the religion out lets people in hospitals and offices try a practice they'd never have tried otherwise, and that ethics can be taught without Buddhist doctrine. Buddhist teachers themselves differ: some welcome the secular programs, some share Purser's worry. Neither side wants less calm. The question is what the calm is for.
screen: `CALM ISN'T THE SAME AS GOOD.` · `ONE STRAND OF AN EIGHTFOLD PATH.` · `NOT HARMING, DOING GOOD, THEN MIND.` · `WHAT IS THE CALM FOR?` · then, large: `NOT JUST CALM.`

segments.voice: Before you settle, choose one small, concrete intention for today in your own words: to speak without harshness in one hard conversation, to notice who's being left out of a meeting, to tell the truth about one small thing. Then rest with the breath, and near the end bring the intention back once and let the quiet you've gathered lean toward it. If you pray, you can offer it there.
Mindfulness without ethics. The critics' worry that a practice sold for productivity can lose the roots that tied it to how you treat people. Today's word.
Your line: not just calm. Calm makes good company for a good intention. Go gently.

1328.title: Mindfulness in schools
1328.hook: a large UK trial found school mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching (Kuyken et al., 2022)
1328.howItsDone: Some schools offer mindfulness lessons as part of their teaching; teachers of contemplative practice often stress that it works best when people choose it rather than being made to do it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mindfulness without ethics, and the question of what calm is for. Your line was not just calm.

Third period, a classroom of teenagers. The teacher dims the lights and asks everyone to close their eyes and notice the breath. A few actually do. One stares at the ceiling tiles. A couple in the back are trying hard not to laugh. Somebody's phone buzzes in a backpack. On paper it's a lovely idea: teach every child, early, the skills adults pay for later. So researchers in the United Kingdom tested it properly, across a great many schools, over years. The answer wasn't the one its supporters hoped for.
screen: `EYES CLOSED, THIRD PERIOD.` → `A LOVELY IDEA ON PAPER.` → `TESTED PROPERLY.`

segments.voice: First, the trial. A team led by Willem Kuyken ran a large study in UK secondary schools. Some schools, chosen at random, taught a mindfulness course with trained teachers. Others kept their usual lessons on social and emotional health. Then the researchers followed the students over time. Second, the result. The mindfulness lessons did no better than the usual teaching for students' mental health. Not worse, not better. The researchers also reported that many students did little of the practice outside class. Third, what that does and doesn't mean. It doesn't show that mindfulness harms young people, or that it does nothing for adults who choose it. It shows something narrower: a practice handed to a whole class, required, on a timetable, didn't do what was hoped. One reading: choosing may matter. Fourth, an old picture of invitation. In the book of Revelation, in the King James text, Jesus speaks to a church this way: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him." Even the one knocking doesn't break the door down. He knocks, and waits, and the door opens from the inside. Some readers hear a whole approach to practice in that picture. A practice offered can be taken up. A practice imposed tends to get endured.

If you pray, you can hold them that way in prayer.
Mindfulness in schools. A large UK trial found mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching, a reminder that a practice can be offered but not imposed. Today's word.
Your line: invite, don't force. The door opens from the inside. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1329.title: Hard experiences
1329.hook: a 2020 review estimated about 8 percent of meditators report unpleasant effects (Farias et al.)
1329.howItsDone: Careful meditation teachers ask students to notice warning signs such as panic, feeling unreal or flooding memories, and to open their eyes, ground themselves, shorten or stop practice, and seek help when those signs appear.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mindfulness in schools: a big trial found required lessons no better than usual teaching. Your line was invite, don't force.

Not every sit ends in peace. Someone closes their eyes for a few minutes of breathing, and instead of quiet, their heart starts racing. Or an old memory they'd packed away comes up with full force. Or the room starts to feel strangely unreal. The cheerful version of meditation skips this part. But it belongs to the honest picture: sometimes practice is hard, and not in a good way. Today, what researchers found, what one old teacher wrote about his own breakdown, and how to know when to stop.
screen: `NOT EVERY SIT ENDS IN PEACE.` → `A RACING HEART, AN OLD MEMORY.` → `THE HONEST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the numbers, carefully. A review led by Miguel Farias pooled studies that asked meditators about unpleasant effects. It estimated that about 8 percent reported at least one; anxiety and low mood were among the most common. That's a minority. But it isn't zero, and it isn't nothing. Second, the old teachers knew. The Japanese Zen teacher Hakuin wrote about his own collapse in a text known as Idle Talk on a Night Boat. As he tells it, he pushed his practice so hard that his body and mind broke down, a condition he called Zen sickness; Zen has its own word for this. A hermit, he says, taught him a gentler practice that helped him recover. Third, the signs. Clinicians who study these experiences describe warning signs worth knowing: panic that builds rather than passes, feeling detached or unreal, painful memories flooding in, sleep falling apart. Their advice is plain: open your eyes, feel your feet, move your body, shorten the sit or stop, and talk to someone. If thoughts of harming yourself ever come, reach out right away: call your local emergency number, or in the US, call or text 988. Fourth, what stopping means. Stopping isn't failing. Hakuin's own story turns on learning a gentler way. Knowing your edge is part of the practice, not a break from it.
screen: `ABOUT 8 PERCENT REPORTED ONE.` · `HAKUIN'S ZEN SICKNESS.` · `PANIC, UNREALITY, FLOODING.` · `STOPPING ISN'T FAILING.` · then, large: `KNOW WHEN TO STOP.`

segments.voice: Keep your eyes open today, resting softly on the floor a little ahead of you, both feet on the ground, breathing normally. Gently ask what your own signs would be, a tight chest, a spinning head, feeling far away, and name one or two quietly. Then make the plan: if that comes, I open my eyes wide, look around the room, press my feet down, and stop.
Hard experiences. A minority of meditators report unpleasant effects, and old teachers wrote about them too. Today's word.
Your line: know when to stop. The way out is always right there, and using it is no failure. Take good care.

1330.title: When to see someone
1330.hook: practice complements, never replaces, medical or psychological care
1330.howItsDone: Meditation teachers and religious communities can encourage people who are struggling to see a doctor or counselor, and to keep practice and prayer alongside professional care rather than instead of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hard experiences, and the signs that say stop. Your line was know when to stop. Today goes one step further.

Open the contacts on your phone and scroll. There's probably a pizza place in there, a plumber, someone from a trip whose last name you've forgotten. Is there a doctor? A counselor? A number to call at three in the morning if things got very dark? If the honest answer is no, the search may have to start on a bad night, when searching is hardest. A week on the honest part of practice ends with a very practical honesty: practice is good company, and it is not a doctor.
screen: `OPEN YOUR CONTACTS.` → `IS THERE A DOCTOR IN THERE?` → `PRACTICE IS NOT A DOCTOR.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Practice complements care. It never replaces it. A practice can sit beside therapy, medicine and a good doctor; it shouldn't stand in for them. Second, the old texts agree. The Jewish sage Ben Sira, whose book is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and in the Apocrypha of some Protestant ones, says, in the King James text: "Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him." In the same chapter he tells the sick to pray, and also to make room for the physician. Both, not either. In Islam, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Some readers take it to mean that seeking treatment is part of faith, not a lack of it. Third, the when. Yesterday's signs that don't pass when you stop. Low mood that settles in for weeks. Not being able to work, sleep or eat. Any thought of harming yourself. Those are reasons to see someone, not to sit longer. In an emergency, call your local emergency number; in the US, you can call or text 988. Fourth, the week: the replication crisis, what held up, too many good results, mindfulness without ethics, mindfulness in schools, hard experiences, and now this. A week of saying where practice ends, so you can trust it where it doesn't.
screen: `COMPLEMENTS, NEVER REPLACES.` · `HONOR THE PHYSICIAN.` · `SIGNS THAT DON'T PASS.` · `A WEEK OF WHERE PRACTICE ENDS.` · then, large: `CARE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: if things got hard, who would I call? Let a face or a place come: a family doctor, a counselor someone once mentioned, a clinic near you, a crisis line. If nothing comes, notice that without judging it; it only means there's one small job to do, and you can breathe with the question for the rest of the sit.
When to see someone. When signs don't pass, mood stays low, or harm crosses your mind, practice steps aside for real care. Today's word.
Your line: care first. Practice is good company, and it is not a doctor. See you tomorrow.
